find: A very common error on 6-mark questions: students say 'covalent bonds break when graphite or diamond melts'. For graphite, the weak intermolecular forces between layers are overcome on melting, not the covalent bonds — this is why graphite still has a very high melting point.
replace: A very common error on 6-mark questions: students say the weak forces between graphite layers explain its high melting point. They do not. Melting diamond or graphite means breaking many strong covalent bonds, which is why both melt at very high temperatures. expect: Step 1 — Mr of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 100 [1 mark]. Step 2 — Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 [1 mark]. Step 3 — Mr of CO₂ = 12 + (2×16) = 44 [1 mark]. Step 4 — Sum of Mr of all products = 56 + 44 = 100 [1 mark]. Step 5 — Atom economy = (56 ÷ 100) × 100 = 56% [1 mark]. Step 6 — Interpretation: 44% of the starting mass becomes CO₂ waste; this is a moderate atom economy and the CO₂ by-product has implications for carbon emissions in industrial lime production [1 mark].
value: Step 1 — Mr of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3×16) = 100 [1 mark]. Step 2 — CaCO₃ is the only reactant, so the total Mr of the reactants is also 100 [1 mark]. Step 3 — Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56 [1 mark]. Step 4 — check with the other product: Mr of CO₂ = 12 + (2×16) = 44, and 56 + 44 = 100, so mass is conserved [1 mark]. Step 5 — Atom economy = (56 ÷ 100) × 100 = 56% [1 mark]. Step 6 — Interpretation: 44% of the starting mass becomes CO₂ waste; this is a moderate atom economy and the CO₂ by-product has implications for carbon emissions in industrial lime production [1 mark].
note: F15: atom-economy denominator is the reactants
